clinicalPearls: A self-limiting non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis of early childhood presenting with multiple small red-brown to yellowish macules and flat-topped papules.
Onset is usually in the first three years of life, with lesions beginning on the head and face, particularly the cheeks, forehead and around the eyes and ears.
Lesions subsequently spread in a cephalocaudal direction to the neck, upper trunk and proximal limbs while sparing mucosae, palms and soles.
The condition is asymptomatic and, by definition, has no visceral, ocular or bony involvement.
Spontaneous resolution over months to a few years is the rule, often leaving transient hyperpigmentation or slight atrophy.

Histology shows a well-demarcated dermal infiltrate of histiocytes that are CD68 positive and CD1a and langerin negative, with characteristic comma-shaped or worm-like bodies on electron microscopy and absence of Birbeck granules.
It is considered by many authorities to lie on a spectrum with juvenile xanthogranuloma and generalised eruptive histiocytosis within the cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses.
Rare reports describe coexistent diabetes insipidus or diabetes mellitus, so evolving systemic symptoms merit review.
reference.pathophysiology: Benign cephalic histiocytosis is a reactive proliferation of dermal macrophage-lineage histiocytes belonging to the cutaneous non-Langerhans cell histiocytoses. The infiltrating cells are dendrocyte-derived histiocytes that express macrophage markers such as CD68 but lack the Langerhans cell markers CD1a and langerin and contain no Birbeck granules; ultrastructurally they show distinctive comma-shaped or worm-like bodies and coated vesicles. Unlike the xanthomatous histiocytoses, the histiocytes contain little or no lipid early in the course, though lipidisation may develop over time, supporting the view that benign cephalic histiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma and generalised eruptive histiocytosis represent overlapping expressions of a single reactive histiocytic process. The self-limiting behaviour reflects eventual clearance of the reactive infiltrate rather than a clonal neoplastic proliferation.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry (CD68, factor XIIIa, CD1a, langerin)
Electron microscopy demonstrating comma-shaped bodies and absent Birbeck granules where diagnosis is uncertain
Clinical review to confirm absence of systemic involvement
Blood glucose and assessment for diabetes insipidus if suggestive symptoms arise
Dermoscopy to distinguish from mastocytosis and other papular disorders
Serial photography to document the characteristic evolution and regression
redFlags: Development of polyuria and polydipsia suggesting diabetes insipidus
Hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy suggesting an alternative systemic histiocytosis
Mucosal, palmar or plantar involvement, which is atypical and should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
Progressive rather than eventually regressing disease
Systemic symptoms such as fever or failure to thrive
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; the eruption is entirely benign and resolves spontaneously over months to several years, usually without residual scarring, and no treatment is required.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the papules as cutaneous mastocytosis or flat warts and instituting unnecessary treatment.
Confusing it with Langerhans cell histiocytosis; immunohistochemistry for CD1a and langerin distinguishes the two.
Subjecting a child to extensive systemic investigation for what is a benign self-limiting condition.
Failing to counsel families that lesions may continue to appear for a time before regression begins.
Overlooking the rare emergence of diabetes insipidus during follow-up.
references: WHO Classification of Histiocytoses and revised histiocytosis classification (current)
Standard paediatric dermatology reference texts (current editions)
management: Reassure that the condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving spontaneously over months to a few years without treatment
Adopt watchful observation with serial photography to document the characteristic evolution and regression
Confirm the absence of visceral, ocular and bony involvement to distinguish it from Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Monitor for symptoms of diabetes insipidus or diabetes mellitus, checking blood glucose if suggestive features arise
Avoid unnecessary or aggressive intervention given the excellent prognosis
Refer to dermatology to confirm the diagnosis by biopsy and immunohistochemistry where clinically uncertain
